# MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents

Mengting Li    Xilong Cheng    Zhihao Xiao    Zhenhua Xu
Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Jingyuan Zhou Affiliation: Guangxi
University    Linfeng Li Affiliation: Beihang University    Long Zhang
Affiliation: Kuaishou Technology
[li.mengting@buaa.edu.cn](mailto:li.mengting@buaa.edu.cn);
[chengzhengyu330@cuc.edu.cn](mialto:chengzhengyu330@cuc.edu.cn,)   
Borui Cai    Yunxiao Qin Affiliation: Communication University of China

###### Abstract

LLM-based role-playing agents are fluent at imitating a character’s
style, yet struggle to make role-consistent decisions over long
narrative horizons. Such decisions are shaped by experiences spanning
many prior scenes, which are often partial and may point in different
directions. Existing methods inject cross-scene memories as context, but
do not reason about how past events shape a character’s current
motivations and behavior. We propose MemRole, a framework that makes
this memory-to-decision process explicit. It introduces Long-Horizon
Memory Thinking (LHMT), a reasoning schema that decomposes hidden
reasoning into context understanding, memory activation, and response
strategy planning, trained on a novel-derived dataset whose
character-grounded, timeline-constrained memory pools limit each
character to what it could plausibly know at the current narrative
point. Beyond supervised fine-tuning, we propose Self-Refining On-Policy
Self-Distillation (SR-OPSD): the model critiques its own rollouts
against the reference under a data-driven rubric, and a
critique-conditioned teacher view of the same model distills token-level
guidance back into the policy. MemRole-32B improves over its backbone by
15.2 points on memory-grounded role-playing, performs on par with
frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.4, and achieves the best
character-motivation recognition accuracy on CroSS-MR.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2611.01778v1/first_cropped.png)

Figure 1: Illustration of Long-Horizon Memory Thinking (LHMT), which
transforms cross-scene memories into a role-consistent response through
three structured stages.

The recent progress of role-playing agents (RPAs) has benefited
substantially from the rapid development of large language models
(LLMs), enabling them to emulate a character’s speaking style,
personality traits, and background knowledge with increasing
fluency ([Shao et al., 2023](#bib.bib3); [Zhou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib13); [Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib4)). Yet fluency is not
fidelity. What ultimately distinguishes a character is not how they talk
in a single turn, but the decisions they make—and a character’s
decisions are rarely determined by the immediate context alone [McAdams
(2011)](#bib.bib19); [Conway and Pleydell-Pearce (2000)](#bib.bib18).
They are shaped by experiences that span many prior scenes: past
humiliations, broken promises, shifting loyalties. A choice that looks
abrupt or even shocking in the moment is in fact driven by this
long-horizon memory, which renders it coherent and, in hindsight, even
inevitable.

We refer to this ability as long-horizon reasoning in role-playing:
reasoning over how memories spanning many prior scenes, often partial
and not always mutually reinforcing, drive a character’s decisions in
the present. At consequential moments, such memory shapes not only what
a character decides, the externally observable action or stance, but
also the motivations and emotions that, though unobservable, are carried
into that decision ([Pillemer, 2003](#bib.bib28); [Graesser et al.,
1994](#bib.bib29)). Yet most existing methods supply cross-scene memory
through retrieval-augmented generation, surfacing relevant past snippets
as supplementary background to reinforce consistency rather than
reasoning about how those events drive the current decision ([Wang et
al., 2024](#bib.bib7); [Ahn et al., 2024](#bib.bib16); [Cheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib30); [Xiao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32)). Approaches that go further still fall short: some
tie memory to the immediate turn ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)), while
others, closest to our setting, reduce role-playing to a multiple-choice
benchmark that scores a character’s choice but leaves the underlying
motivations and emotions unexamined ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)).

Yet fully recovering this implicit long-horizon reasoning from novels is
difficult, demanding a thorough understanding of a character’s traits,
their accumulated memory, and the surrounding situation. The same
history of slights and broken promises may settle into silent resentment
in one character yet escalate into a decisive, irreversible act in
another, and the memories behind such a choice do not always point the
same way: they may reinforce one another, cut against one another, or
bear on the decision in different respects. Supervised fine-tuning can
only imitate a single reference trajectory, and its training signal
never lands on the model’s own generations, leaving the failure modes
specific to its own reasoning unaddressed ([Chu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20)). Reinforcement learning offers an alternative, but
our setting provides little to reward reliably: open-ended role-play
admits no verifiable answer, and an identical surface decision may
follow from a weighing of past memories or merely coincide with it.

The key missing supervision is therefore not whether an agent can access
memory, but how it should transform memory into a decision. Modeling
this transformation requires addressing two challenges at once: first,
the model must learn a reasoning schema that explains how accumulated,
often conflicting memories shape the character’s current motivations,
constraints, and behavioral tendencies; second, training must provide
supervision over this intermediate reasoning process rather than only
judging the final response.

To address these challenges, we propose MemRole, a two-stage framework
that makes the memory-to-decision process explicit and improves it
through critique-guided on-policy self-distillation. First, supervised
cold-start training teaches Long-Horizon Memory Thinking (LHMT), a
three-stage schema of context understanding, memory activation, and
response strategy planning
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"))
that makes explicit how past memories shape the current decision rather
than serving merely as static context. Second, Self-Refining On-Policy
Self-Distillation (SR-OPSD) provides adaptive reasoning-level
supervision: the model critiques its own on-policy rollouts with a
data-driven rubric, and a critique-conditioned teacher view distills
token-level guidance back into the student. In this way, MemRole
supervises the intermediate memory-to-decision process directly, without
reducing feedback to a scalar objective over the final response. The
reference enters only through the critique, never as an imitation
target.

To validate MemRole, we construct MemRole-Dataset, a decision-centered
role-playing dataset built from high-quality novels. We segment each
novel into scenes and build, for each major character, a memory pool of
prior-scene nodes rewritten from their perspective. Anchored to the
scene’s position on the narrative timeline, each pool contains only past
scenes the character could plausibly know, separating what they know
from what they do not. Trained on this data, MemRole substantially
improves memory-grounded role-playing over strong role-playing baselines
while remaining competitive with frontier LLMs.

Our contributions are threefold. (1) We propose MemRole, a framework
that reasons over long-horizon memories to make role-consistent
decisions, combining LHMT with a two-stage training procedure of SFT
followed by SR-OPSD. (2) We construct MemRole-Dataset, a
decision-centered role-playing dataset with character-grounded,
timeline-constrained memory pools. (3) Controlled ablations show that
every LHMT stage and every component of SR-OPSD contributes, with the
largest gains concentrated in memory activation and in the data-driven
rubric.

## 2 Related Work

#### LLM-based Role-Playing Agents

Prior studies mainly relied on prompt engineering or supervised
fine-tuning (SFT) to imitate character-specific styles and background
knowledge ([Shao et al., 2023](#bib.bib3); [Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib4)). Since surface-level imitation is insufficient for
maintaining character consistency in complex scenarios, recent studies
have explored reasoning-augmented training for RPAs, including
structured reasoning in CogDual and HER ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib5);
[Du et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)) and RL-based optimization in MOA and
RAIDEN-R1 ([Liao et al., 2025](#bib.bib6); [Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib8); [Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib33)). These methods
improve character imitation and response consistency, but largely reason
within the current turn rather than over a character’s accumulated
history.

#### Memory for Role-Playing Agents

To sustain consistency across scenes, prior work equips role-playing
agents with character memories, typically by retrieving past snippets
and injecting them as supplementary context ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib7); [Ahn et al., 2024](#bib.bib16); [Cheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10); [Ji et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)). Existing methods
typically treat memory as a flat collection for context injection,
rather than a logical basis for reasoning about the character’s state.
We instead build per-character, timeline-constrained memory pools and
train the model to reason explicitly over how these memories shape a
character’s present decision.

#### On-Policy Distillation

Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from teacher to student
models, and recent on-policy variants supervise the student on its own
generated trajectories to mitigate the train–test distribution
mismatch ([Gu et al., 2024](#bib.bib2); [Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12); [Song and Zheng, 2026](#bib.bib1)). A closely related
line internalizes reasoning through information-asymmetric
self-distillation, where one model acts as both student and teacher and
the asymmetry arises from differing input contexts rather than
parameters ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib14); [He et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)). We adapt this paradigm to long-horizon memory
reasoning: rather than exposing reference solutions directly, we
condition the teacher view on per-rollout critiques distilled from the
reference, yielding fine-grained supervision for memory-guided
role-playing decisions.

## 3 MemRole Dataset

### 3.1 Why the MemRole Dataset Is Needed

Long-horizon memory reasoning imposes three requirements on the
underlying data, none of which is jointly satisfied by existing
role-playing corpora
(Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.1 Comparison with Existing Datasets ‣ Appendix A Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")).
First, memory must be _cross-scene and traceable_: a character’s present
decision is driven by events from many prior scenes, so memory cannot be
reduced to a static profile ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib7); [Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)) or to the local surrounding context ([Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib4); [Du et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)). Second, scenes must be
_decision-centered_: studying how memory becomes decision requires turns
where a character makes consequential, character-driven choices, taking
a stance, selecting an action, resolving a value conflict, or reaching a
turning point, rather than turns dominated by incidental exchange.
Third, memory must respect the character’s _epistemic boundary_: a
character can only reason from what it could plausibly know at the
current narrative point, a constraint absent from prior datasets that
retrieve by surface relevance ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib4)) or align
responses with a static character graph ([Cheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)).

As summarized in
Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.1 Comparison with Existing Datasets ‣ Appendix A Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
prior datasets satisfy at most one of these requirements; profile- and
attribute-alignment corpora align with static character dimensions
rather than reasoning over how past events shape present choices, and
decision-oriented benchmarks ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)) evaluate
the final choice while supervising neither memory nor reasoning. Other
lines are orthogonal to our goal: large-scale synthetic corpora ([He et
al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)) prioritize role
coverage over traceable narrative memory, while general-domain and
multi-agent frameworks ([Gao et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Xu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib25)) target hallucination control and scene orchestration
rather than memory-driven decision-making.

### 3.2 Data Curation

![Refer to caption](2611.01778v1/MenRole.png)

Figure 2: Overview of our framework. Left (Data Construction): The
pipeline for constructing the MemRole dataset, involving chapter-scene
segmentation, decision-dense scene filtering, and character-grounded
memory pool creation. Middle (Training): A two-stage optimization
procedure comprising SFT warm-up on validated reasoning traces and
SR-OPSD refinement (bottom), which aligns the model with critique-aware
teacher distributions. Right (Evaluation): Simulated role-playing and
multi-dimensional evaluation on the MemRole Test benchmark.

MemRole is constructed from high-quality novels through a multi-stage
pipeline
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Data Curation ‣ 3 MemRole Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
left) that yields _scene–focal character_ instances, each pairing a
decision-dense scene with the focal character’s profile and a
per-character, timeline-anchored memory pool; the training target is the
LHMT trace followed by the visible response. We first segment each novel
into chapters and scenes and extract structured scene information,
dialogue, and character-centric metadata; all interaction turns are
extracted from the original text rather than freely generated,
preserving narrative authenticity. Two design choices make the resulting
instances decision-bearing rather than incidental: decision-density
filtering and decision-outcome masking.

#### Decision-density filtering.

To ensure that every instance carries a genuine decision signal, we use
an LLM to score whether the focal character makes explicit,
character-driven decisions in a scene, and retain only samples above a
decision-density threshold. This prioritizes scenes with stance-taking,
refusals, commitments, and narrative turning points over filler
dialogue.

#### Decision-outcome masking.

Role-playing setups commonly place a scene introduction and character
motivation in the system prompt, which often already disclose the focal
character’s eventual choice and the scene’s outcome. A model can then
reproduce the behavior from the prompt rather than reason toward it. To
ensure the response is genuinely _inferred_ rather than recoverable from
the prompt, we clean the model-visible context so that it retains only
the situational conditions and other characters’ triggering behaviors,
while removing any content that reveals the focal character’s decision,
its motivation-as-given, or the resulting outcome.

Additional details on the dataset and its construction pipeline are
provided in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

### 3.3 Memory Pool Construction

The memory pool is the core data structure of MemRole. For each
scene–focal character pair, we construct a dedicated pool of $`N`$
nodes, where each node corresponds to a prior scene that may shape the
focal character’s current motivations, beliefs, relationships, or
behavioral tendencies. Each node is an LLM-generated,
_character-perspective_ summary linked to its source scene_id, so that
every memory is traceable to the original narrative and reflects what
that character experienced rather than an omniscient account.

#### Candidate scoping.

To keep the pool within the character’s epistemic boundary, candidate
scenes must satisfy two constraints: _temporal validity_—the scene
occurs before the current scene, preventing future-knowledge leakage;
and _character grounding_—the focal character is physically present, not
merely mentioned by others. Together these ensure the pool contains only
information the character could plausibly know at the current narrative
stage.

#### Memory selection.

Within the scoped candidates, we select nodes via a two-step
LLM-assisted process: a coarse ranking that produces an initial relevant
list, followed by a fine ranking based on pairwise comparisons. To let
the pool grow with the candidate set while avoiding inflation, we retain
the top-$`k`$ candidates under a dynamic cap:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
k=\min\!\left(N,\ \big\lceil b+\alpha\cdot\max(0,\,N-b)\big\rceil\right),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`b`$ is a base size guaranteeing enough memories for small
candidate sets and $`\alpha\in(0,1)`$ is a sub-linear growth rate that
lets the pool expand slowly as candidates accumulate. A sensitivity
analysis of the retrieval budget is provided in
Appendix [E.5](#A5.SS5 "E.5 Analysis of Memory Retrieval ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

### 3.4 Dataset Statistics

MemRole comprises 75 novels, 2,000 character profiles, 14,844 scenes,
and 181,137 role-playing dialogue turns
(Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ A.2 Dataset Overview ‣ Appendix A Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")).
To prevent narrative leakage, we split at the book level so that all
scenes from the same novel fall into the same split. On average, each
turn activates 0.721 memories; among turns with activated memories,
65.03% integrate multiple memories whose effects are *aligned*,
*opposed*, or *mixed*
(Table [7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ A.2 Dataset Overview ‣ Appendix A Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")),
highlighting the need for multi-memory integration beyond single-event
retrieval.

## 4 Method

### 4.1 Long-Horizon Memory Thinking

MemRole addresses this need with Long-Horizon Memory Thinking (LHMT), a
decision-oriented reasoning schema that makes the memory-to-decision
process explicit. As shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Data Curation ‣ 3 MemRole Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")(left)
, LHMT decomposes long-horizon memory reasoning into three ordered
components: *context understanding*, *memory activation*, and *response
strategy planning*, which are written as natural-language paragraphs in
an auxiliary \<think\> block before the visible character response.

#### Context Understanding.

This stage analyzes the character’s current state, the interactional
demands of the dialogue, and the character-profile information relevant
to the current turn, thereby clarifying what the response needs to
accomplish.

#### Memory Activation.

This stage determines whether the current turn needs to consult the
memory pool. If so, the model selects memories relevant to the current
decision and reasons about how they shape the character’s motivations,
constraints, and behavioral tendencies. When multiple memories are
relevant, the model further integrates their aligned, conflicting, or
complementary effects to derive a memory-grounded decision tendency for
the current turn.

#### Response Strategy Planning.

Given input $`x=(C_{t},P,M_{r,s})`$, where $`C_{t}`$ is the dialogue
context, $`P`$ the character profile, and
$`M_{r,s}=\{m_{1},\dots,m_{n}\}`$ the memory pool of character $`r`$ in
scene $`s`$, the model generates
$`o_{t}=[T_{t};y_{t}]\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$, i.e., an LHMT
trace $`T_{t}`$ followed by the visible response $`y_{t}`$.

### 4.2 Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation for LHMT

#### SFT warm-up with synthesized LHMT traces.

Since LHMT traces are not available in the original novel corpus, we
synthesize them with a generator–validator distillation pipeline
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Data Curation ‣ 3 MemRole Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
left). For each focal-character turn, a generator LLM produces a
candidate LHMT trace $`T_{t}`$ grounded in the dialogue context, role
prompt, memory pool, and original response $`y_{t}`$, without copying
the response into the trace.

A validator LLM filters candidates with a validation checklist covering
structural validity, memory grounding, memory-need consistency, and
leakage risks. Validated traces are used for supervised warm-up, with
further details in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B LHMT Trace Construction Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

We first perform supervised fine-tuning on a mixture of LHMT-augmented
role-playing trajectories and general instruction-tuning data, as
detailed in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 SFT Data Mixture ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").
For an LHMT-supervised example with input $`x=(C_{t},P,M_{r,s})`$ and
target output $`o^{*}=[T_{t};y_{t}]`$, the objective is the standard
next-token negative log-likelihood:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\sum_{j=1}^{|o^{*}|}\log\pi_{\theta}(o^{*}_{j}\mid x,o^{*}_{<j}).
``` |  | (2) |

We denote the resulting model as $`\pi_{A}`$. In SR-OPSD, we initialize
the trainable policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ from $`\pi_{A}`$ and keep another
copy of $`\pi_{A}`$ frozen as the critique model and teacher view. We
empirically validate this choice against alternative critique models in
Appendix [C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 Validation of the Critique Model ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

#### Data-driven Rubric Construction.

SR-OPSD uses a critique rubric to diagnose weaknesses in the policy’s
own generations. Rather than manually specifying the rubric, we induce
it from the empirical error patterns of the SFT warm-up model
$`\pi_{A}`$(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Data Curation ‣ 3 MemRole Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
middle). Specifically, we sample $`M`$ rollouts
$`\{\hat{o}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{M}`$ from $`\pi_{A}`$ and compare each
rollout with its reference output $`o^{*(i)}`$ to collect a weakness
corpus $`\{w^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{M}`$.

The weakness corpus is then consolidated through an offline hierarchical
summarization process into a global pool of $`L`$ critique dimensions:

|     |                                  |     |
|-----|----------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{R}=\{d_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L},
       ```                               |     |

where each $`d_{l}`$ denotes a recurring weakness dimension. The rubric
remains fixed during SR-OPSD training, while the critique model
dynamically selects and instantiates the relevant dimensions for each
on-policy rollout. Details are provided in
Appendix [C.7](#A3.SS7 "C.7 Data-driven Rubric Construction ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

#### Critique-aware Rollout Diagnosis.

Let $`\mathcal{D}=\{(x,o^{*})\}`$ denote the LHMT-supervised training
set used for SR-OPSD. In each training iteration, given
$`(x,o^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}`$, the policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ first samples
an on-policy trajectory:

|     |                                                         |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{o}=[\hat{T};\hat{y}]\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x),
       ```                                                      |     |

where $`\hat{T}`$ is the generated LHMT trace and $`\hat{y}`$ is the
generated role-playing response. The frozen $`\pi_{A}`$ then receives
$`(x,\hat{o},\mathcal{R},o^{*})`$ and, guided by $`\mathcal{R}`$,
generates a structured critique $`c`$ that identifies the rubric
dimensions in which $`\hat{o}`$ deviates from $`o^{*}`$. Details are
provided in
Appendix [C.8](#A3.SS8 "C.8 SR-OPSD Critique Prompt ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

Consistency (SC), Anthropomorphism (AN), Character Fidelity (CF),
Storyline Quality (SQ), Memory Activation Quality (MAQ), and Reasoning
Consistency (RC). Life Choice evaluates persona-consistent
decision-making with given motivation, while Cross-MR evaluates
character-motivation recognition accuracy.

#### Asymmetric Self-Distillation.

SR-OPSD performs information-asymmetric self-distillation on the policy
model’s own rollout $`\hat{o}`$
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Data Curation ‣ 3 MemRole Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
middle). The student view predicts each next token using only the
original input $`x`$ and the on-policy prefix $`\hat{o}_{<j}`$:

|     |                                                     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{S}^{(j)}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{o}_{<j}).
       ```                                                  |     |

In contrast, the teacher view uses the same on-policy prefix but
additionally conditions on the structured critique $`c`$ as privileged
context:

|     |                                                  |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{T}^{(j)}=\pi_{A}(\cdot\mid x,c,\hat{o}_{<j}).
       ```                                               |     |

We then minimize the token-level KL divergence on the policy model’s own
rollout:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SR\text{-}OPSD}}=\frac{1}{|\hat{o}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|\hat{o}|}\mathrm{KL}\left(p_{T}^{(j)}\,\|\,p_{S}^{(j)}\right).
``` |  |

At inference time, the model uses only the original input $`x`$, without
access to $`o^{*}`$ or the critique model. The complete SR-OPSD training
procedure is provided in
Appendix [C.4](#A3.SS4 "C.4 SR-OPSD Training Algorithm ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

#### Models.

We compare MemRole with strong commercial LLMs, open-source general
LLMs, and role-playing baselines. MemRole is fine-tuned from Qwen3-8B
and Qwen3-32B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)). We use
Gemini-3-Pro-Preview as the environment model for generating interactive
contexts and as the next-speaker prediction (NSP) model.

#### Metrics.

Following CoSER ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib4)), we use GPT-5.5 to
evaluate simulated role-playing conversations across four general
role-playing dimensions: Storyline Consistency (SC), Anthropomorphism
(AN), Character Fidelity (CF), and Storyline Quality (SQ). To better
assess long-horizon memory reasoning, we further introduce two
MemRole-specific metrics: Memory Activation Quality (MAQ) and Reasoning
Consistency (RC)
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Data Curation ‣ 3 MemRole Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
right). Memory Activation Quality evaluates activation accuracy,
activation sufficiency, and usage appropriateness, while Reasoning
Consistency evaluates causal consistency, behavioral continuity, and
motivational rationality. For LifeChoice and Cross-MR, we report
accuracy. Detailed rubrics are provided in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

#### Benchmarks.

We evaluate models on four complementary benchmarks. MemRole Test
evaluates long-horizon memory-grounded role-playing, while CoSER ([Wang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib4)) evaluates general role-playing quality in
established-character simulations. For MemRole Test and CoSER, we
evaluate 200 conversations containing 20 interaction turns. Following
the evaluation protocol of CoSER ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib4)), we
score only the externally observable responses in these open-ended
conversations, excluding reasoning traces. To provide complementary and
more objective evaluations of character decision-making, we further
include two multiple-choice benchmarks. LifeChoice ([Xu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11)) evaluates persona-consistent decision-making on 1,000
multiple-choice instances, while CroSS-MR ([Yuan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27)) evaluates character-motivation recognition on all 445
instances. Detailed dataset statistics and evaluation rubrics are
provided in
Appendices [A](#A1 "Appendix A Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")
and [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
respectively.

### 5.2 Main Results

As shown in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Critique-aware Rollout Diagnosis. ‣ 4.2 Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation for LHMT ‣ 4 Method ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
MemRole substantially improves memory-grounded role-playing over its
backbone models and prior role-playing baselines. MemRole-32B achieves
an average score of 64.25 on MemRole Test, outperforming Qwen3-32B by
15.20 points and obtaining the highest MAQ score among all evaluated
models. MemRole-8B also improves over Qwen3-8B by 10.39 points and
surpasses both CoSER-8B and CoSER-70B, showing that the gains are not
merely due to model scale.

On CoSER, MemRole-32B achieves competitive overall performance and the
highest Storyline Quality score in our CoSER evaluation; full results
are reported in
Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Full Results on the CoSER Benchmark ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").
On LifeChoice, MemRole-32B remains competitive, indicating that the
proposed memory-reasoning training preserves general persona-driven
decision-making ability. On CroSS-MR, MemRole-32B achieves the highest
accuracy of 69.83, outperforming Qwen3-32B by 20.22 points.

We further assess evaluation robustness through alternative-judge
scoring and pairwise comparisons with randomized response order. Both
analyses yield broadly consistent comparative conclusions
(Appendices [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Evaluation with Different LLM Judges ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")
and [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Pairwise Preference Evaluation ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")).

### 5.3 Human Evaluation

We recruit 20 evaluators familiar with narrative role-playing to assess
anonymized responses from six representative LLMs on 100 randomly
selected MemRole test samples using a 1–10 scale. As shown in
Table [13](#A4.T13 "Table 13 ‣ D.3 Human Evaluation ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
MemRole-32B achieves the highest human score (7.02) and pairwise win
rate (72.3%), outperforming Qwen3-32B, HER-RL, and CoSER-70B. MemRole-8B
also outperforms Qwen3-8B. We further assess human–automatic alignment
on 300 responses and 300 LHMT traces using case-level agreement, Cohen’s
$`\kappa`$, and Spearman’s $`\rho`$. The results show strong agreement
for both responses (89.4%, $`\kappa=0.77`$, $`\rho=0.81`$) and LHMT
traces (90.2%, $`\kappa=0.80`$, $`\rho=0.83`$). Detailed results are
provided in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Human Evaluation ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")

### 5.4 Ablation Study

#### Effect of LHMT components.

We ablate each LHMT component to assess its contribution. As shown in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Effect of SR-OPSD training. ‣ 5.4 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
removing any component degrades performance. Removing memory activation
causes the largest Memory drop ($`-10.1`$), highlighting its central
role in long-horizon grounding. Removing response strategy planning
mainly hurts Dialogue ($`-5.2`$), while removing context understanding
leads to smaller but consistent drops ($`-3.2/-3.9`$), suggesting that
it provides useful scaffolding for later reasoning.

#### Effect of SR-OPSD training.

The training-stage ablations show that each part of SR-OPSD contributes
to performance. Standard OPSD, which directly conditions the teacher on
the full reference, provides modest gains over SFT ($`+1.5/+1.4`$).
Replacing direct reference conditioning with rollout-specific critiques
further improves performance ($`+1.1/+2.2`$), and the data-driven rubric
yields the final gain ($`+2.3/+4.0`$), indicating that rubric-guided
critiques provide more targeted supervision for memory-to-decision
reasoning.

### 5.5 Analysis of LHMT Reasoning

We analyze LHMT in terms of schema effectiveness, supervision-trace
validity, and the quality of model-generated reasoning traces.

#### Effectiveness of the LHMT Schema.

We evaluate LHMT at both prompting and training levels. For prompting,
we conduct a zero-shot experiment on frozen Qwen3 models, comparing
Direct Response (no explicit reasoning), Generic CoT (free-form
step-by-step reasoning), and LHMT Prompting (three-stage structured
reasoning). As shown in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Effectiveness of the LHMT Schema. ‣ 5.5 Analysis of LHMT Reasoning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")(a),
LHMT performs comparably to Generic CoT on 8B but shows a greater
advantage on 32B. For training, we compare Direct-response SFT,
Generic-CoT SFT, and LHMT SFT under matched settings, using identical
instances, target responses, data mixtures, and optimization
configurations. Generic-CoT traces use the same teacher and generation
setup as LHMT traces, differing only in reasoning structure.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Effectiveness of the LHMT Schema. ‣ 5.5 Analysis of LHMT Reasoning ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")(b)
shows that Generic-CoT SFT improves over Direct-response SFT by 1.56,
1.67, and 2.33 points in Dialogue Avg., MAQ, and RC, respectively. LHMT
SFT yields further gains of 1.06, 1.71, and 1.49 points, respectively.
Additional results across Dense RAG and GraphRAG are provided in
Appendix [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Generalization across Memory Backends ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

| Qwen3-8B | Direct Response | 42.44 | 42.03 | 42.38 |

|  | LHMT Prompting | 43.87 | 44.78 | 44.34 |

#### Quality of Supervision Traces.

To assess whether LHMT traces reflect narrative-supported decisions
rather than plausible post-hoc explanations, we sample 2,000 instances
from the training set containing explicit decision evidence, such as
internal monologues or stated motivations. Given the current context,
candidate memories, their source passages, and the LHMT trace, an
automatic judge evaluates Context Faithfulness, Memory Grounding, and
Plan Coherence, with acceptance rates of 90.4%, 93.4%, and 88.9%,
respectively. A trace is considered fully valid only when all three
dimensions meet the quality criteria without contradicting the
character’s explicit thoughts, knowledge, or narrative timeline.
Overall, 84.4% of the traces meet this standard. Human validation of the
judge is reported in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Human Evaluation ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

#### Quality of Generated Traces.

We evaluate LHMT trace quality along three dimensions: Context
Faithfulness, Memory Grounding, and Plan Coherence, using the same 300
test turns for all models. All three dimensions improve from Base + LHMT
prompt through SFT warm-up to SR-OPSD. Memory Grounding remains the
weakest after SFT but improves the most under SR-OPSD, becoming
comparable to the other two. This suggests that critique-aware
refinement particularly strengthens memory-to-decision reasoning,
consistent with the largest degradation observed when ablating memory
activation
(Appendix [E.6](#A5.SS6 "E.6 Quality of Generated LHMT Traces ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")).

## 6 Conclusion

We presented MemRole, which trains role-playing agents to reason from
long-horizon memories to role-consistent decisions by combining the LHMT
schema with critique-guided on-policy self-distillation (SR-OPSD),
together with a dataset of character-grounded, timeline-constrained
memory pools. Experiments and ablations show consistent gains over
backbones and role-playing baselines, highlighting the value of
supervising intermediate memory reasoning.

## Limitations

MemRole has two main limitations. First, LHMT trace synthesis,
critique-rubric construction, and automatic evaluation rely on LLM
assistance. We mitigate potential noise with structured prompts,
independent validation, and human expert calibration, while stronger
validators or broader human auditing could further improve robustness.
Second, MemRole studies reasoning over pre-existing narrative memories
from novels, which provides a controlled setting for memory-to-decision
modeling. Extending the framework to online memory acquisition and
revision during user interaction remains future work.

## Ethics Statement

This work studies long-horizon memory reasoning for fictional
role-playing agents. The dataset is constructed from literary narratives
and centers on fictional characters, scenes, and character memories; it
does not use private user conversations, personally identifiable
information, or real-person profiling. Because the source novels may
contain copyrighted text and socially biased or sensitive portrayals, we
will not redistribute raw copyrighted content. Instead, we will release
only copyright-compliant derived resources, such as annotations,
prompts, statistics, and model outputs, for research purposes. We also
acknowledge that stronger role-playing agents may be misused for
deceptive impersonation, emotionally manipulative interaction, or unsafe
fictional simulation. Therefore, systems based on this work should be
deployed with clear AI disclosure, content safeguards, and appropriate
human oversight. This work is intended for research on fictional
narrative reasoning, not for simulating real individuals without consent
or making decisions that affect real people.

### A.2 Dataset Overview

MemRole is a long-horizon memory-based role-playing dataset constructed
from raw novel corpora. As shown in
Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ A.2 Dataset Overview ‣ Appendix A Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
the final dataset contains 75 novels, 2,000 character profiles, 14,844
scenes, and 181,137 role-playing dialogue turns. Each scene contains an
average of 12.20 dialogue turns, and each turn activates 0.721 memories
on average. Each sample is centered on a focal character in a specific
scene and includes the current dialogue context, the original character
response, the character profile, and a long-horizon memory pool.

We split the dataset at the book level to prevent narrative leakage
between training and test sets. The final split contains 64 training
novels and 11 test novels, with all scenes, characters, and dialogue
samples from the same novel assigned to the same split.

We further report memory-use statistics.

### A.3 Dataset Construction Pipeline

We curate MemRole through a multi-stage extractive pipeline that goes
from raw novel text to a structured, queryable representation. The
details are as follows.

#### Source Selection.

To ensure narrative quality and character depth, we start from the top
1,000 books in Goodreads’ “Best Books Ever” list and use an LLM-based
screening process to select novels better suited for long-horizon
role-playing decision modeling. We prioritize books with sustained
character arcs, decision-rich interactions, and cross-scene causal
chains.

After this screening process, we obtain 75 novels for dataset
construction. The selected novels cover a broad range of genres,
including fantasy, historical fiction, science fiction, romance,
mystery, literary fiction, adventure, young adult fiction, dystopian
fiction, and gothic fiction. This genre coverage introduces diverse
narrative styles, social settings, interpersonal conflicts, and
character decision patterns, making MemRole suitable for studying
long-horizon role-playing behavior across varied story worlds.

#### Chapter and Scene Segmentation.

We first segment each book into chapter-level chunks based on its
chapter structure. Chapter boundaries are jointly identified by rules
and LLMs, and then globally adjudicated to produce a unified chapter
list with chapter-level summaries. Within each chapter, we use LLMs to
extract candidate scenes and their metadata, followed by global
adjudication to obtain non-overlapping scene segments that fully cover
the chapter.

#### Data Extraction.

We use LLMs to extract structured information from each scene, including
location, in-story time, atmosphere, relevant characters, preceding
context, scene summary, scene outcome, and dialogue content. Following
the message representation in CoSER, we further organize dialogue
content into three types of information: character speech, actions, and
thoughts.

To filter decision-dense samples, we compute heuristic indicators such
as dialogue density, action/thought ratios, and the number of
interaction turns, and assign each scene an interaction-type label
accordingly. We then combine these labels with the LLM-assessed
role-playing value to select high-quality scenes with sufficient
character interaction, explicit behavioral choices, and strong
plot-advancing effects.

#### Character Data Organization.

Based on the extracted scenes and dialogues, we construct a character
profile for each major character. We first perform alias resolution with
LLMs, mapping different character mentions to a canonical name. Each
character profile is then organized into three core components: a static
profile, including personality traits, core values, speech style, and
behavioral patterns; relationships, recording relation types,
relationship trajectories, and the scene_ids of several key scenes; and
a dynamic character arc, which partitions the character’s narrative
trajectory into 3–7 stages.

Each stage is associated with a scene_id range, a set of key
turning-point scene_ids, and a state snapshot describing the character’s
situation, goals, known plot facts, and important relationship states
during that stage. This stage-wise structure makes character memory
queryable: given any decision point, we can trace back to the preceding
character stages and further locate relevant scenes for memory
retrieval.

## Appendix B LHMT Trace Construction Details

### B.1 Reasoning Data Synthesis for LLM Role-play

Since LHMT traces do not explicitly appear in the original novel corpus,
we construct a generator–validator distillation pipeline to synthesize
high-quality auxiliary reasoning traces for role-play training. The
pipeline preserves the original character response while using it as a
grounding signal for trace construction. Specifically, a generator LLM
first produces a candidate LHMT trace, and a validator LLM then checks
the candidate against a set of validation rules summarized from failed
generations and manually inspected error cases. According to the
validation result, the candidate is either accepted, revised with
feedback, or discarded.

#### Stage 1: Candidate trace synthesis.

For each focal-character turn $`t`$, we keep the original target
response $`y_{t}`$ unchanged and ask the generator LLM to synthesize an
auxiliary LHMT trace $`T_{t}`$ conditioned on $`(C_{t},P,M_{r,s})`$. The
resulting training output is written as

|     |                      |     |
|-----|----------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       o_{t}=[T_{t};y_{t}].
       ```                   |     |

Here, $`T_{t}`$ follows the three-paragraph LHMT format defined in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Long-Horizon Memory Thinking ‣ 4 Method ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").
The target response $`y_{t}`$ is provided to the generator only as a
grounding signal, so that the generated trace can be aligned with the
observed character behavior. It is not copied verbatim into the trace,
nor is the trace allowed to reveal surface wording from $`y_{t}`$.

#### Stage 2: Validator-guided verification and retry.

After a candidate trace is generated, we use a validator LLM to assess
whether it satisfies the required LHMT properties. The validation
criteria are derived from common failure patterns observed in
preliminary generations and are further refined through manual
inspection. The validator checks whether the trace: (i) follows the
required LHMT structure; (ii) grounds its reasoning in the role prompt,
dialogue context, and available memory pool; (iii) correctly determines
whether memory activation is needed and which memories should be
activated; (iv) distinguishes stable character-profile knowledge from
episodic scene memory; and (v) avoids leaking future information or
copying surface expressions from the target response.

The validator returns one of three decisions: PASS, REVISE, or REJECT. A
candidate marked as PASS is retained as the final trace. For REVISE, the
validator provides a concise description of the weaknesses, and the
generator is prompted again with the original input, the previous
candidate, and the validator feedback to regenerate the trace. For
REJECT, the candidate is treated as invalid and resampled. This
generate–validate–retry process is repeated until the candidate passes
validation or reaches the maximum number of attempts. In our
implementation, we allow at most three generation attempts for each
turn; samples that still fail validation after the final attempt are
dropped from the supervised warm-up data.

#### Stage 3: Sequential trace integration.

The synthesis process proceeds sequentially within each multi-turn
dialogue. When constructing the trace $`T_{t}`$ for the $`t`$-th
focal-character turn, the generator can additionally condition on
previously validated traces from earlier turns in the same dialogue.
This helps maintain consistency in multi-turn reasoning, especially for
memory activation and character-state tracking. This sequential
construction context is used only during data synthesis. In the final
training and inference settings, the model is not given hidden reasoning
traces from previous turns as visible dialogue history. Finally, each
validated trace $`T_{t}`$ is inserted immediately before its
corresponding target response $`y_{t}`$, yielding training trajectories
with explicit LHMT supervision.

### B.2 LHMT Trace Generation and Validation Prompts

This appendix presents the reference prompts used in our LHMT trace
construction pipeline. The generation prompt, shown in
Table [20](#A5.T20 "Table 20 ‣ E.7 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
asks the teacher LLM to prepend an auxiliary LHMT trace to the original
role-playing response. The validation prompt is split into two parts for
readability:
Table [21](#A5.T21 "Table 21 ‣ E.7 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")
lists the validation criteria, and
Table [22](#A5.T22 "Table 22 ‣ E.7 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")
specifies the structured JSON output used to guide revision or retry
before adding the trace to the supervised warm-up data.

## Appendix C Training and Implementation Details

### C.1 SFT Data Mixture

During supervised warm-up, we train on a mixture of LHMT-augmented
role-playing trajectories and general instruction-tuning data. The
LHMT-augmented trajectories provide direct supervision for learning the
memory-to-decision reasoning format, while the general data helps
preserve the model’s general reasoning and instruction-following
capabilities.

Specifically, the final SFT mixture contains 50% LHMT-augmented
trajectories and 50% Tulu instruction-tuning data.

### C.2 SFT Training Setup

We initialize the base policy from the corresponding backbone model and
fine-tune it on the SFT mixture described in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 SFT Data Mixture ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").
For LHMT-supervised examples, the target sequence contains both the
auxiliary LHMT trace and the visible response; for general data, it
follows the original response format. All models are trained with the
standard next-token prediction objective.

We use LoRA for efficient fine-tuning, with rank $`r=8`$, $`\alpha=16`$,
dropout 0.05, and adapters applied to all linear modules. The main
hyperparameters for Qwen3-8B are listed in
Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.2 SFT Training Setup ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

|                         |                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------|
| Hyperparameter          | Value                    |
| Backbone model          | Qwen3-8B                 |
| Maximum sequence length | 8192                     |
| Learning rate           | 1.0e-4                   |
| Batch size (Global)     | 128                      |
| Number of epochs        | 8                        |
| Optimizer               | AdamW (DeepSpeed ZeRO-3) |
| Warmup ratio            | 10%                      |
| Weight decay            | 0.01                     |
| Precision               | bfloat16 (bf16)          |

Table 9: Main hyperparameters for supervised warm-up.

### C.3 SR-OPSD Implementation

After supervised warm-up, we denote the resulting model as $`\pi_{A}`$.
In SR-OPSD, the trainable policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ is initialized from
$`\pi_{A}`$, while another copy of $`\pi_{A}`$ is kept frozen as the
critique model and teacher view. At each step, $`\pi_{\theta}`$ samples
an on-policy trajectory $`\hat{o}`$ from the original input.

The frozen critique model receives $`(x,\hat{o},\mathcal{R},o^{*})`$ and
generates a structured critique $`c`$. The reference output $`o^{*}`$ is
used only for critique construction and is not directly exposed to the
teacher view. The teacher view conditions on $`c`$ as privileged
context, while the student view receives only $`x`$ and its own rollout
prefix. We optimize the student with token-level KL divergence on the
policy’s own rollout.

The critique is used only during training and is not available during
inference. The main SR-OPSD hyperparameters are shown in
Table [10](#A3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ C.3 SR-OPSD Implementation ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

|                              |                    |
|------------------------------|--------------------|
| Hyperparameter               | Value              |
| Initial policy               | $`\pi_{A}`$        |
| Critique / teacher model     | Frozen $`\pi_{A}`$ |
| Rollout sampling temperature | 1.0                |
| Maximum rollout length       | 2048               |
| Learning rate                | 1.0e-5             |
| Batch size (Global)          | 128                |
| Number of SR-OPSD steps      | 100                |

Table 10: Main hyperparameters for SR-OPSD.

### C.4 SR-OPSD Training Algorithm

1: SFT warm-up model $`\pi_{A}`$ (frozen), rubric $`\mathcal{R}`$,
training data $`\mathcal{D}`$

2: Trained policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$

3: Initialize $`\pi_{\theta}\leftarrow\pi_{A}`$

4: for each training step do

5:   Sample $`(x,o^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}`$, where $`x=(C_{t},P,M_{r,s})`$
and $`o^{*}=[T_{t};y_{t}]`$

6:   $`\hat{o}=[\hat{T};\hat{y}]\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$
$`\triangleright`$ on-policy LHMT trajectory

7:   $`c\leftarrow\pi_{A}(x,\hat{o},\mathcal{R},o^{*})`$
$`\triangleright`$ critique by frozen $`\pi_{A}`$; $`o^{*}`$ only for
critique construction

8:   for each token position $`j=1,\ldots,|\hat{o}|`$ do

9:    $`p_{T}^{(j)}\leftarrow\pi_{A}(\cdot\mid x,c,\hat{o}_{<j})`$
$`\triangleright`$ teacher: frozen $`\pi_{A}`$ with critique $`c`$

10:    $`p_{S}^{(j)}\leftarrow\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{o}_{<j})`$
$`\triangleright`$ student: trainable $`\pi_{\theta}`$, no critique

11:   end for

12:
  $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SR\text{-}OPSD}}\leftarrow\frac{1}{|\hat{o}|}\sum_{j=1}^{|\hat{o}|}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{T}^{(j)}\,\|\,p_{S}^{(j)}\right)`$

13:   Update $`\pi_{\theta}`$ via
$`\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SR\text{-}OPSD}}`$

14: end for

15: return $`\pi_{\theta}`$

Algorithm 1 SR-OPSD Training (Phase 2)

### C.5 Validation of the Critique Model

In the default SR-OPSD configuration, the frozen SFT model $`\pi_{A}`$
serves as both the critique model and the teacher view. To evaluate its
suitability for critique generation, we conduct a controlled experiment
under the MemRole-8B setting. We keep the student initialization,
teacher view, SR-OPSD training data, and optimization settings fixed,
and vary only the frozen model used to generate critiques.

We compare four critique models: the Qwen3-8B backbone, an SFT model
trained without the general-data mixture, the frozen $`\pi_{A}`$ used in
our default configuration, and Qwen3-32B. In all variants, the teacher
view and student initialization remain unchanged.

As shown in
Table [11](#A3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ C.5 Validation of the Critique Model ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
the frozen $`\pi_{A}`$ outperforms Qwen3-8B and the variant without
general-data mixing, while Qwen3-32B provides only modest further gains.
These results support using the frozen $`\pi_{A}`$ as an effective and
efficient critique model.

### C.6 Inference

At inference time, the model receives only the standard role-playing
input, including the current dialogue context, character profile, and
long-horizon memory pool. Training-only components, including reference
responses, validators, the critique model, and critique texts, are
excluded.

For generation, we use nucleus sampling with a temperature of 0.75, a
top-$`p`$ value of 0.9, and a repetition penalty of 1.05. We set the
maximum number of newly generated tokens to 4,096, allowing the model to
generate the auxiliary LHMT trace before the visible response. Unless
otherwise specified, we remove the auxiliary LHMT trace and evaluate
only the final visible role-playing response.

### C.7 Data-driven Rubric Construction

This section details the rubric construction procedure summarized in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Self-Refining On-Policy Self-Distillation for LHMT ‣ 4 Method ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").
We construct the rubric in two stages: collecting empirical weaknesses
from $`\pi_{A}`$’s rollouts and consolidating these weaknesses through
hierarchical summarization into a global pool of critique dimensions.

#### Stage 1: Weakness corpus collection.

We sample $`M=20{,}000`$ turn-level rollouts from the SFT warm-up model
$`\pi_{A}`$ on a reserved subset of the LHMT training split. Each
rollout corresponds to one focal-character turn, where $`\pi_{A}`$
generates a complete output
$`\hat{o}^{(i)}=[\hat{T}^{(i)};\hat{y}^{(i)}]`$ given the input
$`x^{(i)}=(C_{t}^{(i)},P^{(i)},M_{r,s}^{(i)})`$. To cover diverse
failure modes, we stratify sampling by memory-activation count. For each
rollout $`\hat{o}^{(i)}`$ paired with its reference output
$`o^{*(i)}=[T_{t}^{(i)};y_{t}^{(i)}]`$, we prompt GPT-5.5 to compare the
two and extract a structured weakness list $`w^{(i)}`$. Each $`w^{(i)}`$
contains free-form weakness descriptions with severity labels, specific
failures, and abstract improvement directions. These categories are not
predefined; they are later consolidated into the final critique
dimensions.

#### Stage 2: Hierarchical summarization.

We consolidate the raw weakness corpus into a structured rubric through
a two-step hierarchical summarization process. At the block level, the
weakness corpus is divided into smaller subsets, and GPT-5.5 summarizes
each subset into candidate weakness dimensions with brief definitions
and empirical support counts. These support counts are used only to
guide consolidation, not as training-time loss weights. At the global
level, GPT-5.5 merges semantically overlapping candidates, removes
overly specific dimensions, and retains dimensions that recur across
different subsets.

The final rubric is denoted as

|     |                                  |     |
|-----|----------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{R}=\{d_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L},
       ```                               |     |

where each $`d_{l}`$ represents a recurring weakness dimension. In our
implementation, the final rubric contains $`L=12`$ dimensions covering
memory use, character consistency, and reasoning quality. The full list
of dimensions, with definitions and example failure cases, is provided
in
Table [12](#A3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Stage 2: Hierarchical summarization. ‣ C.7 Data-driven Rubric Construction ‣ Appendix C Training and Implementation Details ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  Category |  Rubric dimension |  Definition |  Typical failure |
|  Memory |  Memory-need misjudgment |  Fails to correctly decide whether the current turn requires consulting the memory pool. |  Uses memory when the current context is sufficient, or ignores memory when past events are needed. |
|  Memory |  Missing relevant memory |  Fails to activate a memory that is necessary for explaining the character’s current decision. |  Omits a prior confrontation or promise that should constrain the response. |
|  Memory |  Irrelevant memory injection |  Activates memory entries that are unrelated to the current decision or unsupported by the input. |  Grounds the response in an unrelated past scene. |
|  Memory |  Multi-memory effect integration error |  Fails to integrate aligned, conflicting, or complementary effects across multiple activated memories. |  Treats conflicting memories as independently supportive, or ignores their combined effect. |
|  Character |  Motivation misalignment |  Misidentifies the character’s current motivation, constraint, or behavioral tendency. |  Makes a cautious character act boldly without contextual support. |
|  Character |  Character voice inconsistency |  Produces a response whose style, register, emotional tone, or manner of expression is inconsistent with the character. |  Uses overly modern, generic, or emotionally mismatched phrasing. |
|  Character |  Relationship or stance inconsistency |  Fails to preserve the character’s current relationship state or stance toward other characters. |  Responds warmly to a character they currently distrust. |
|  Character |  Information-disclosure error |  Reveals, withholds, or frames information in a way inconsistent with the character’s knowledge, intent, or social situation. |  Exposes a secret or hidden plan that the character should avoid revealing. |
|  Reasoning |  Shallow context understanding |  Misreads the immediate dialogue pressure, scene dynamics, character relationships, or response need. |  Treats a tense confrontation as a casual factual exchange. |
|  Reasoning |  Response strategy planning error |  Fails to plan the appropriate response stance, form, tone, or information-disclosure boundary. |  Chooses the wrong response form, such as direct confession when restraint is needed. |
|  Reasoning |  Trace–response inconsistency |  The visible response does not faithfully execute the plan stated in the LHMT trace. |  The trace plans restrained denial, but the response becomes openly confrontational. |
|  Reasoning |  Premature or unsupported plot reasoning |  Introduces future knowledge, retrospective interpretation, or unsupported plot information unavailable at the current turn. |  Mentions an outcome or hidden fact that the character could not yet know. |

Table 12: Final critique dimensions used in SR-OPSD. The rubric contains
12 recurring weakness dimensions induced from empirical errors of the
SFT warm-up model, grouped into memory-related, character-related, and
reasoning-related categories.

### C.8 SR-OPSD Critique Prompt

Table [23](#A5.T23 "Table 23 ‣ E.7 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")
presents the critique-generation prompt used in SR-OPSD. The prompt

### D.2 Scoring Rubrics

Following the methodology of CoSER ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib4)), we
use an LLM-based judge to evaluate open-ended role-playing conversations
on MemRole Test and CoSER. Each dimension is scored on a 0–100 scale,
where higher scores indicate better role-playing quality. The evaluation
covers four CoSER-style dimensions:

#### Storyline Consistency.

This dimension assesses whether the simulated conversation is consistent
with the original narrative context. It focuses on whether the model’s
responses, including emotions, attitudes, and behaviors, remain faithful
to the ongoing storyline.

#### Anthropomorphism.

This dimension assesses whether the role-playing agent behaves in a
human-like manner. It considers self-identity, emotional depth, persona
coherence, and social interaction.

#### Character Fidelity.

This dimension assesses how well the model reflects the target
character. It focuses on whether the generated responses are consistent
with the character’s personality, linguistic style, knowledge,
relationships, and behavioral patterns.

#### Storyline Quality.

This dimension assesses the overall naturalness and quality of the
simulated conversation. It focuses on narrative flow, logical
consistency, and whether the dialogue develops coherently.

For LifeChoice, we evaluate whether the model selects the decision
consistent with the ground-truth character choice. We report accuracy as
the primary metric.

### E.2 Evaluation with Different LLM Judges

To examine whether our conclusions depend on the preferences of a single
LLM judge, we re-score the same model outputs using GPT-5.5,
Claude-4.6-Opus, and DeepSeek-V3.2. All judges receive identical
evaluation inputs and follow the same scoring rubric and evaluation
protocol.
Table [16](#A5.T16 "Table 16 ‣ E.2 Evaluation with Different LLM Judges ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")
reports the average scores assigned by the three judges.

Although the judges differ in their absolute scoring scales, they
produce broadly consistent comparative results. In particular,
MemRole-32B consistently outperforms the representative role-playing
baselines under all three judges. Its advantage over HER-RL is 11.41
points under GPT-5.5, 11.42 points under Claude-4.6-Opus, and 13.08
points under DeepSeek-V3.2. MemRole-8B also remains competitive with
HER-RL, slightly trailing it under GPT-5.5 but outperforming it under
the other two judges. These results indicate that the observed gains are
robust to judge choice rather than being an artifact of the preferences
of a single evaluation model.

### E.4 Generalization across Memory Backends

To examine whether LHMT is tied to the specialized memory representation
used in MemRole, we evaluate its generalization across different memory
backends. Specifically, we replace the character-grounded memory pool
with two commonly used retrieval architectures: Dense RAG and GraphRAG.

For Dense RAG, we segment the character-accessible prior scenes into
textual chunks and retrieve evidence relevant to the current scene and
dialogue context. For GraphRAG, we organize the same historical
narrative into a graph containing character, event, and relationship
information, and retrieve relevant nodes and their textualized local
neighborhoods. The MemRole backend uses the character-perspective,
timeline-constrained memory nodes described in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Memory Pool Construction ‣ 3 MemRole Dataset ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents").

For a fair comparison, all backends use the same historical corpus, test
instances, backbone model, evidence-token budget, and decoding
configuration, and access only character-available information prior to
the current scene.

For each memory backend, we compare three inference modes: *Direct
Response*, which directly generates the role-playing response from the
retrieved evidence; *Generic CoT*, which performs free-form step-by-step
reasoning before generating the response; and *LHMT Prompting*, which
organizes the reasoning process into context understanding, memory
activation, and response strategy planning. The backbone remains frozen
in all settings, and only the reasoning instruction is changed.

As shown in
Table [18](#A5.T18 "Table 18 ‣ E.4 Generalization across Memory Backends ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
LHMT Prompting consistently improves memory reasoning across alternative
backends. Compared with Generic CoT, it improves Dialogue Avg. by 0.22
and 0.26 points, MAQ by 0.73 and 0.74 points, and RC by 0.92 and 0.96
points under Dense RAG and GraphRAG, respectively. With the MemRole
Pool, LHMT achieves comparable dialogue quality while improving MAQ and
RC by 0.52 and 1.23 points. These results suggest that LHMT provides a
robust memory-to-decision reasoning interface across both textual and
graph-based retrieval architectures.

### E.5 Analysis of Memory Retrieval

By default, MemRole dynamically determines the number of retrieved
memories for each scene–character instance using an adaptive memory cap.
To evaluate the model’s sensitivity to the retrieval budget, we fix the
model, test instances, and retrieval ranking, and vary only the maximum
number of retrieved memories $`K`$ visible to the model. When fewer than
$`K`$ valid memories are available, all available memories are used.

As shown in
Figure [3](#A5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ E.5 Analysis of Memory Retrieval ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents"),
performance improves substantially as $`K`$ increases from 0 to 5, with
Dialogue Avg. increasing by 3.18 points, after which the gains begin to
plateau. Compared with $`K=5`$, increasing the budget to $`K=10`$ yields
only modest improvements of 0.61, 1.14, and 0.32 points in Dialogue
Avg., MAQ, and RC, respectively. Further increasing $`K`$ to 20 reduces
Dialogue Avg., MAQ, and RC by 0.81, 0.26, and 1.11 points, respectively.
Dialogue Avg. denotes the average of SC, AN, CF, and SQ.

These results suggest that a small set of top-ranked memories captures
most of the information relevant to character decisions, whereas a
larger retrieval budget may introduce weakly relevant evidence. This
finding is consistent with our adaptive memory-cap design: the base
parameter is set to $`b=5`$ to capture most of the performance gains,
while the cap grows sub-linearly with the number of valid candidates,
allowing the retrieval budget to expand moderately for instances with
richer relevant histories.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: Sensitivity of MemRole-8B to the maximum number of retrieved
memories. Dialogue Avg. denotes the mean of SC, AN, CF, and SQ. Most of
the gain is obtained by $`k=5`$, after which performance plateaus;
increasing $`K`$ to 20 degrades all three metrics.

are reported on the 8B backbone. Higher is better.

### E.7 Training Dynamics

Figure [4](#A5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ E.7 Training Dynamics ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ MemRole: From Memories to Decisions for Long-Horizon Reasoning in Role-Playing Agents")
shows that SR-OPSD rapidly improves over the SFT baseline within the
first 30 training steps and then remains consistently higher throughout
training. The curve stabilizes after about 50–60 steps with moderate
variance across three runs, suggesting that SR-OPSD provides stable
gains without severe training collapse.

The \<think\> block must contain exactly three natural paragraphs:    Paragraph 1:  Analyze the focal character’s current situation, immediate interaction pressure, and only the profile traits relevant to this turn.    Paragraph 2:  Decide whether the scene memory pool is needed. The scene memory pool refers only to memories listed under Relevant Past Memories, not the character profile. When multiple memories are used, determine whether their effects are aligned, opposed, or mixed, and explain their combined effect. Paragraph 3:  Describe the response policy, including the appropriate use of speech, action, or inner thought, the tone, what should be revealed or withheld, and what should be avoided.    Rules:  1. Use third-person analysis rather than first-person narration.  2. Use exactly three natural paragraphs without headings, bullets, numbered steps, or explicit reasoning tags.  3. Ground every claim in the reference context, listed memories, character relationships, or the original target.  4. Do not invent facts or use future information unavailable to the character.  5. Use the original target only to infer the intended stance and response policy. Do not quote, closely paraphrase, or pre-announce its distinctive wording, actions, or thoughts inside \<think\>.  6. Distinguish stable profile knowledge from episodic scene memories.  7. After \</think\>, append the original assistant target exactly unchanged.    Return only:    \<think\>  Natural paragraph 1.    Natural paragraph 2.    Natural paragraph 3.  \</think\>  {target_assistant_content} |

You will receive:  (1) the reference context,  (2) the original assistant target, and  (3) a generated assistant value containing a \<think\> block followed by the target.    === REFERENCE CONTEXT ===  {reference_content_with_memories}    === ORIGINAL ASSISTANT TARGET ===  {target_assistant_content}    === GENERATED ASSISTANT VALUE ===  {generated_reasoning}    Determine whether the generated \<think\> is valid supervision for current-turn memory-aware role-playing.    Check the following:    1. Structure  - There is exactly one \<think\> block containing three natural paragraphs.  - The assistant target after \</think\> exactly matches the original target.  - The reasoning contains no headings, bullets, numbered steps, or explicit reasoning tags.    2. Grounding and temporal validity  - Every claim is grounded in the profile, current scenario, dialogue prefix, listed memories, character relationships, or original target.  - The reasoning contains no fabricated facts or future information unavailable to the character at the current turn.    3. Memory decision  - Independently determine whether the listed scene memory pool is needed.  - Do not treat character-profile information as scene memory.  - When memory is needed, verify the selected memory ids and explain the behavioral pressure of each memory.  - For multiple activated memories, classify their combined effect as aligned, opposed, or mixed.  - When memory is not needed, verify that the current context and profile are sufficient.    4. Target leakage  - The reasoning may use the target to infer the intended stance and response policy, but must not quote, closely paraphrase, or pre-announce its distinctive wording, actions, thoughts, or withheld information.    5. Training usefulness  - The reasoning clearly explains the current information need, memory relevance, and response policy.  - It is not generic or merely a restatement of the target. |
